name: Fixed appliances with elastics

lead: Fixed appliances are brackets bonded to the teeth and joined by an archwire. Elastics are small rubber bands hooked between the upper and lower sets of brackets to add a pulling force across the bite. In orthodontic practice they are used to move teeth so that the upper and lower arches fit together, which affects how the teeth, lips and profile look.

In looksmaxxing discussion the topic comes up mostly as a comparison: proponents of orthotropics and 'mewing' warn that braces, extractions and headgear can pull the teeth back and flatten the face, while orthodontists generally describe braces with elastics as a standard, well-studied way to correct bites. Research includes studies that compare elastics with functional appliances such as the Herbst.

paras: Patients wear fixed braces for roughly one to three years, and the orthodontist prescribes elastics on specific hooks, usually changed daily by the patient. Elastics come in different sizes, strengths and colours. They are typically used in the later phases of treatment, after the teeth are aligned, and are often followed by a retainer.

Fixed braces make plaque control harder and can cause gum inflammation, and tooth movement causes some root shortening in most cases, which is rarely serious. Soreness after adjustments is common. Elastics only work when worn consistently. Critics in the orthotropic community say conventional treatment, especially with extractions, may restrict facial development; mainstream orthodontics regards that view as unproven.

angle.text: Fixed braces with elastics move teeth into alignment and correct how the upper and lower arches meet, which changes the visible smile and the support of the lips. People choose it to fix crooked teeth, overjets and underbites without surgery.

lead: Fixed appliances with elastics is a form of orthodontic treatment in which brackets bonded to the teeth are linked by an archwire, and small rubber bands are stretched between the upper and lower arches to correct how the jaws meet. People use it to straighten teeth, close gaps and adjust the bite (for example reducing an overjet), which changes the smile and the way the lips and lower face are supported. [1][2]

Elastics attach to hooks on the brackets or archwire; their placement is set by the treatment plan, and they come in a range of diameters, strengths and colours. [2] They are the traditional way of delivering force across the bite in Class II and Class III cases, and studies of Class II treatment often use elastics as the comparison group for newer functional appliances. [1]

The topic is debated in looksmaxxing and orthotropic circles. John Mew, who developed orthotropics, concluded that extractions, fixed appliances and headgear could harm facial growth, and he argued that crooked teeth reflect posture and environment more than genetics; mainstream orthodontics attributes malocclusion mainly to genetics and describes his evidence as inadequate. [3]

paras: Dental braces consist of brackets, bands and an archwire; springs or rubber bands add force in a specific direction when the plan calls for it. [2] Elastics hook onto the brackets and span the gap between the upper and lower teeth, pulling the arches toward a corrected relationship. [2]

Edward Angle's early twentieth-century classification of bites into Class I, II and III remains the framework used to decide which elastics are prescribed, and Calvin Case and Henry Albert Baker are credited with pioneering the use of rubber elastics in that period. [2]

Orthodontic patients seek braces for straighter teeth, a more even smile and a better-fitting bite. In Class II cases, where the upper teeth sit forward of the lower, elastics are used alongside braces to move the arches into a more normal relationship. Open-bite cases are also treated with fixed appliances and elastics, sometimes with added devices such as expanders and mini-implants. [4]

Orthotropics, developed by British orthodontist John Mew, holds that facial form is shaped by oral posture and growth guidance. Mew believed from clinical observation that extractions, fixed appliances and headgear could harm facial growth, and his 1958 'Tropic Premise' framed malocclusion as a postural problem that early intervention could prevent. [3]

Mainstream orthodontics generally attributes crooked teeth mainly to genetics and regards the evidence for orthotropic treatment as inadequate. [3] Online, the debate is often phrased around whether braces 'retract' the face; this is discussed from the orthotropic side as a claim, and orthodontic bodies have not accepted it. [3]

Fixed braces can cause visible plaque, gum inflammation and recession, particularly when cleaning is poor. Pain after adjustments rises with the force applied, and a 2017 Cochrane review found moderate-quality evidence that analgesics reduce it. Some root resorption occurs in most cases, and it is rarely serious. [2]

A three-dimensional study of Class II patients compared skeletal changes with the Herbst appliance against control patients treated with elastics, and examined whether results differed by vertical facial pattern. [1]
A practice-based research network study described the clinicians and patients in a large cohort examining recommendations and treatment for adult anterior open bite. [4]
No published trial has tested the specific claim made in orthotropic circles that fixed appliances with elastics retract the face compared with orthotropic methods.
